paragraphs: Rav Shmuel son of Rav Yitzchak.

His father was very pious, as in Jerusalem Talmud Rosh Hashanah 1:4: he fasted two days of Yom Kippur (because of doubt) and died through this. In Jerusalem Talmud Challah 1:1, Hyman identifies the reading בר אבוי דשמואל בר״י as erroneous.
He is mentioned in Eruvin 97a: “for the father of Rav Shmuel son of Rav Yitzchak taught.”
In Jerusalem Talmud Shevuot, chapter 4, end of halakhah 1: “Rabbi Yirmeyah, Rabbi Shmuel son of Rav Yitzchak in the name of Rav Yitzchak, who said in the name of Rav.”

His son Rav Shmuel still merited to receive from Rav, as in Niddah 64b, where he said, “It was explained to me by Rav himself.” Hyman also lists the abbreviated form “R′ Shmuel son of Rav Yitzchak said that Rav said” at Berakhot 14b and 59a, Shabbat 51a, Pesachim 113b, Yevamot 46a and 97a, Gittin 78a, Bava Metzia 41a, Bava Batra 119a, and Jerusalem Talmud Pesachim 7:12.

When Rav Huna became academy head and all of Rav’s students sat before him, he too sat before Rav Huna, as in Eruvin 36a, where he asked Rav Huna. He taught before Rav Huna, as in Bava Batra 113b. He asked Rav Huna, as in Jerusalem Talmud Rosh Hashanah, chapter 3, end of halakhah 2.

In Niddah 6b: “Rav Huna said: The twenty-four-hour [retroactive] period of a niddah … Rav Nachman said to him: But it was taught … Rav Shmuel son of Rav Yitzchak accepted it from him: regarding unconsecrated food prepared in the purity of holy things” (Rashi explains: he accepted this refutation from Rav Nachman). Hyman infers from this that he sat in the company of Rav Nachman and Rav Huna, and this was when Rav Huna headed the academy, as explained in his entry.

Hyman cites Megillah 8a: “He taught before Rav Huna … Rava said to him: If so.” He treats “to him” as a scribal error and proposes “Rava said,” arguing that Rava did not meet Rav Huna. The matching exchange in the consulted Davidson text appears on 8b.
In Bava Kamma 43b: “He raised an objection … Rabbah said to him: Thus it teaches”, which Hyman places when they all sat before Rav Huna.

In Hyman’s account, when he was already one of the great men of the generation, his heart moved him to go up to the Land of Israel to attain perfection in the service of the Creator. Therefore, although Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish were then in the Land of Israel, he did not always sit in their company and did not want to show them his greatness in Torah; rather, he was humble and lowly, occupied in the service of the Lord, and was holy and pure, as in Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot 2:4 and Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin, chapter 10, end of halakhah 2, where the maidservant of Rabbi Shmuel son of Rav Yitzchak said: “In all my days I never saw a bad thing on my master’s garments.”
He would bring joy to bride and groom, as in Ketubot 17a, where he would dance [juggling] with three [branches] before them.
In Jerusalem Talmud Peah 1:1, folio 3b, it is stated more explicitly that he would take myrtles and dance with them before the bride, and Rabbi Zeira said: “The elder is shaming us.”

Rav Shmuel bar Yehudah said of him and of Rabbi Zeira that they were the two great men of the generation, as in Gittin 23b. There he was friendly with all the great students of Rabbi Yochanan, such as Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, whom Rav Shmuel asked, as in Menachot 47a, and whom Rav Shmuel addressed as “my teacher,” as in Chullin 98a (Hyman explains that Rabbi Chiyya was not his teacher and that Rav Shmuel used the address only out of humility).
When Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba died, he accepted mourning, and ate meat and drank wine, as in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 3:1, folio 2b.
In Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot 12:2 [it is related] that he had a case and sent Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba.
In Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot, chapter 3, end of halakhah 1, when Rabbi Assi wanted to go abroad, he told him that he must ask Rabbi Yochanan.
Rabbi Assi spoke in his name, as in Tamid 31b.

In Jerusalem Talmud Rosh Hashanah 3:1: Rabbi Huna (the second) knew testimony for a certain person; [that person] went to be judged before him, and [the other party] denied it against him. Rabbi Shmuel son of Rabbi Yitzchak said to him: “Because you know that Rabbi Huna is a great man, you deny it against him?” (Hyman considers it undoubted that both had sat before Rav Huna in Babylonia.)

He was likewise friendly with Rabbi Abba, as in Sukkah 3a; with Rabbi Ami, as in Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot 15:4, whom he called a distinguished man; and with Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Abba bar Mamal, as in Makkot 13b; with Rabbi Zeira, as in Pesachim 72b, where both sat at the gate of Rabbi Shmuel son of Rabbi Yitzchak and were sitting and saying, “Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said,” etc.; and Rabbi Zeira asked him, Pesikta deRav Kahana, supplied locator קמב. (142.; pagination not established here). Their disputes: Zevachim 65b and Niddah 9b.

Likewise he disagrees with Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Chanina, as in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 3:5. His sayings and halakhot we find in Eruvin 81b, on Rav Huna’s words; Pesachim 85b; Yoma 26a, resolving an objection to Rabbi Yochanan’s statement; Megillah 2a; Ketubot 3a, where he said, “If there are fixed courts, a woman may marry on any day”; Ketubot 27a; Kiddushin 45b; and Avodah Zarah 75a. His precious words in aggadah we find in Eruvin 95b, where he said, “There is room on the head to place two tefillin”; in Pesachim 49b he adds to the words of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani and says, “and from his back”; likewise in Chagigah 5b he disagrees with Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani and says: “What is ‘because of pride’? Because of the pride of Israel that was taken from them and given to the nations of the world.” In Taanit 17a he gave the reason why the High Priest must have his hair cut from Shabbat eve to Shabbat eve.

In Bava Batra 15b he said: “Whoever took a perutah from Job was blessed.” In Sanhedrin 109b: “Jacob prayed for mercy,” etc. There, 110a: “This teaches that each one suspected his wife with regard to Moses.” In Chullin 56b: “This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, created [bodily] foundations in a person,” etc.
His students and those who speak in his name:
Rabbi Berekhyah son of Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Simon in his name, as in Bereshit Rabbah 53:8; Hyman says the reading should be “Rabbi Berekhyah in the name of Rabbi [Yehudah son of Rabbi Simon].”
Rabbi Huna in his name, as in Jerusalem Talmud Chagigah 1:7 (he is Rabbi Huna II).
Rabbi Chaggai asked him, as in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 2:6.
Rabbi Chanan in his name, as in Jerusalem Talmud Sheviit 6:1.
Rabbi Chananyah in his name, as at the end of Jerusalem Talmud Shabbat, chapter 10, and Tanchuma, Noach 2.
Rabbi Yehoshua HaKohen son of Rabbi Nechemyah in his name, as in Midrash Tehillim, beginning of chapter 80.
Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yose in his name, as in Jerusalem Talmud Rosh Hashanah 1:2.
Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Bun in his name, as in Jerusalem Talmud Maaser Sheni 4:3.

Rabbi Yirmeyah in his name, as in Jerusalem Talmud Peah 1:1, Jerusalem Talmud Eruvin 1:1, additional locator ה., Jerusalem Talmud Chagigah 1:7, and Jerusalem Talmud Shevuot, chapter 4, end of halakhah 2.

Rabbi Meyasha said to him, “Did not our master teach us thus?” as at the end of Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot, chapter 2. Of his family we find only that he had a daughter who married Rav Hoshaya, as in Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 1:1. Of his death we find in Ketubot 17a that a pillar of fire separated between him and everyone else, and there is a tradition that it separates only for one or two in a generation; and Rabbi Zeira said: “His branch helped the elder.”
Rabbi Yirmeyah was present at his death, as in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot, chapter 3, end of halakhah 1, and Jerusalem Talmud Nazir 7:8, where he asked Rabbi Zeira before his bier.

In Jerusalem Talmud Peah 1:1, folio 3b: when he died, a heavenly voice went out that they should go out to do kindness with him, and fire came down and became like a branch of fire between his bier and the congregation.

In Jerusalem Talmud Avodah Zarah 3:1: when he died, cedars were uprooted in the Land of Israel. They said that he used to take a branch and praise before the bride, and a heavenly voice went out and said: “Woe, for Rabbi Shmuel son of Rabbi Yitzchak, the doer of kindness, has died.”
In Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 3:1, additional locator כ. [kept literally]: when he died, Rabbi Zeira accepted mourning and ate lentils.

Rav/Rabbi forms remain scoped to Hyman and each named witness. Fable’s Menachot47a/Chullin98a actor correction is accepted: Shmuel asks Chiyya and calls him my teacher; Hyman explains the address as humility, not actual discipleship. Niddahמע״ל is the twenty-four-hour retroactive period. The named GuggenheimerJTRH3:1 has full RavChuna; Hyman calls this man RabbiHunaII. The litigant seeks judgment before Huna and the other party denies; Shmuel objects that Huna can testify elsewhere, not that Huna testified before himself. The final undoubted Babylonian-school inference remains Hyman’s. Source p014 andp036 say he accepted mourning and ate meat/wine orlentils; GuggenheimerJTBer3:1 instead says he received the mourners and SERVED THEM that food. This comparison is disclosed without silently repairing Hyman’s wording. Source p016 says Assi should askYochanan; the matching named edition has Yasa already asking and Shmuel saying the question still needs answering. Pesachim49b explicitly has ומגבו=fromhisback, not wedge; the violent saying is source speech. Hyman’s Berekhyahבש״ר emendation is retained as a proposal with the continuation [Yehudah sonofSimon]; TEBerR53:8 still supplies the filial-looking chain, so no biography merge follows. Megillah8a/7b supplied exchange was not located by bounded lexical checks and remains held; מהרין in p020 is only provisionally interpreted as explaining and remains held. These questions were already reported by Fable and are not discarded by accepting other corrections. In p002 בר אבוי is kept literally as Hyman’s erroneous reading, not a new person barAvoi. All prior chronology/identity/conjectural claims and copyright are preserved.

Additional digital checks: Davidson Megillah 8b contains the Rav Huna/Rav Shmuel teaching followed by אמר ליה רבא אלא מעתה; the earlier nonmatches on 7b and 8a remain valid within their limited scopes. This identifies a parallel without validating Hyman’s correction of the wording or his chronology. Davidson Yoma 26a has Rav Shmuel explain the contradictory lot-drawing baraita as referring to Shabbat; that context supports the provisional “explaining” but cannot settle the supplied מהרין letters. All inherited edition differences and source holds remain.

The positive Megillah 8b parallel names Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak, without the extra Rav before the father found in this entry’s heading, and retains “Rava said to him.” Hyman’s supplied 8a locator, his insistence that the reading should be “Rava said,” and his chronological argument remain his report; the parallel does not establish that correction or a personal identification. Earlier nonmatch statements describe the recorded bounded checks, not proof that a passage is absent from a page. Yoma 26a places the Shabbat explanation after objections to Rabbi Yochanan’s lot-drawing ruling; it supports the provisional sense of “explaining,” not the supplied מהרין letters. Both source holds remain.

The checked Rosh Hashanah 1:4 and Challah 1:1 paragraphs both speak of the father of Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak fasting two days and dying; the checked Challah text does not display Hyman’s reported בר אבוי error. Eruvin 97a leaves Shmuel untitled. The cited sayings use both Rav and Rabbi, and both bar Yitzchak and bar Rav Yitzchak. The checked Berakhot 59a and Gittin 78a paragraphs do not include “said Rav”; the intended Bava Batra 119a chain remains unconfirmed in the bounded routing. Hyman’s list is retained as his list, not a claim that all named editions have an identical chain.

In the checked Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot 15:4 paragraph, Shmuel gives Ami as the example of a distinguished person, which determines the direction of the English phrase. The checked Niddah 6b context names Huna’s statement and Nachman’s objection. Bava Kamma 43b also gives an alternative in which the questioner answers his own objection, alongside the version in which Rabbah replies; Hyman selects the latter. The Ketubot 17a paragraph is followed by alternative forms for “his branch,” “his folly,” and “his method”; Hyman’s branch wording is retained.

Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot’s closing chapter-two paragraph positively has Meyasha address Shmuel as his teacher. The checked Sanhedrin chapter-one passage calls Hoshaya his son-in-law; Hyman supplies the daughter formulation and literal 1:1 locator. The final Shabbat chapter-ten paragraph positively has Chananyah transmit in Shmuel’s name. The intended transmission was not matched in the wholly checked standard or Buber Noach 2 sections; that separate Tanchuma pointer remains Hyman’s report. The checked beginning of Midrash Tehillim 80 has Yehoshua HaKohen bar Nechemyah in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak, rather than the Shmuel attribution supplied here. The intended Rosh Hashanah 3:2 question, Shevuot 4:2 transmission, Pesikta deRav Kahana קמב. pagination, and Nazir 7:8 pointer remain unconfirmed by these bounded checks; the last lookup returned 404. None establishes an absence from the work or authorizes repairing Hyman’s Hebrew or locators.

Sheviit 6:1 names Chanin where Hyman has Chanan. The checked Bereshit Rabbah 53:8 retains the filial-looking Berekhyah chain beside Hyman’s forceful proposed transmission emendation. The current mixed note’s distinctions about serving mourners, Yasa already asking Yochanan, Rav Chuna versus Hyman’s Rabbi Huna II, and Hyman’s humility and undoubted-schooling inferences remain in force. The named-source comparisons do not admit a common identity, genealogy, teacher network, chronology, or legal ruling. No printed-page correction history or OCR certification is claimed.

The earlier notes describe the evidence before the printed page was checked. Hyman’s vol. III, p. 1139, prints Megillah 8a and quotes “Rava said to him” across the column break. In the consulted Davidson text, Megillah 8b names Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak teaching before Rav Huna and then reads אמר ליה רבא (“Rava said to him”). The pronoun has no named addressee in that clause. The proposed removal of “to him” and the chronology are Hyman’s argument.

Hyman’s print, vol. III, p. 1140, reads מתרץ דברי ר׳ יוחנן, while the supplied Hebrew reads מהרין. In Yoma 26a, Rabbi Yochanan says the morning lottery assigned the service for both the morning and the afternoon daily offerings. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak answers the objection from a source with two lotteries by explaining that it concerns Shabbat, when the priestly watch changes. Rashi explains that the morning watch does not serve in the afternoon. The English follows the printed wording and the supplied Hebrew remains as transcribed.
